analysis.one_liner: Sends monthly cash payments to families with children, replacing the child tax credit and earned income tax credit.
analysis.headline: Introduced November 20, 2025 with 10 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, where it has had no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new monthly cash payment for every child under 19 in the United States, sized to the gap between the poverty line for a single person and a two-person household (roughly $450 per child per month at recent guideline levels), paid through the Social Security Administration. Families would be signed up automatically when they get their child a Social Security number or when the IRS shares dependent data, unless they opt out. To help cover the cost, the bill ends the child tax credit and the earned income tax credit and replaces them with smaller credits: $700 per adult dependent over 18 and $700 for each adult aged 19 to 64 ($1,400 for couples), phasing out above modest incomes. The payments would not count as income for any other benefit, so families would not lose food or housing assistance because of them.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children under 19 gain a guaranteed monthly payment that reaches the poorest households regardless of whether the parents work or owe taxes. Low- and moderate-income adults aged 19 to 64 and people supporting adult dependents gain new refundable credits. The heaviest gains go to families with little or no earnings, who today often get little from the child tax credit.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a monthly cash payment for every child under 19 residing in the U.S. who is a citizen or qualified immigrant, set at one-twelfth of the annual gap between the HHS poverty guideline for a two-person household and for a single person — roughly $450 per child per month at recent guideline levels.

Signs children up automatically: an application for a child's Social Security number, or identification through IRS data sharing, counts as an application unless the family opts out — designed to reach poor families who miss out on tax credits they never claim today.

The payments are disregarded as income for every federal program and any state or local program funded with federal money, so receiving them cannot cost a family SNAP, housing assistance, or other aid.

Replaces the child tax credit and earned income tax credit with a $700 credit for each dependent over 18 and a $700 credit ($1,400 for joint filers) for adults aged 19 to 64, phasing out at 5% above $20,000 of income ($40,000 for couples), with the amounts indexed to inflation.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The bill contains no revenue increases or spending cuts to offset the cost of the new monthly payments and credits; it simply ends the two existing credits, which only partially covers the new spending, so the remainder would add to the federal deficit.

drawbacks.text: It terminates the earned income tax credit, which pays working parents several thousand dollars a year — a parent with two children can currently receive around $7,000 — far more than the $700-per-adult credit that replaces it, so some moderate-wage working families could end up with less total support than they get today.
The bill has no funding mechanism: it raises no revenue and cuts no other spending, so the full cost of universal child payments plus the new adult credits would land on the federal deficit.
Only citizens and 'qualified aliens' qualify, leaving out children who are neither — including undocumented children and some lawfully present children — even though they live in the United States.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the poorest families this is a clear gain: the payment reaches children regardless of their parents' earnings, is worth far more than today's partially refundable child tax credit, and cannot cause a loss of other benefits. The serious trade-offs are that abolishing the earned income tax credit could leave moderate-wage working parents worse off than they are now, and that the bill attaches no funding, so the cost piles onto the deficit. A better-designed version would fund the program and phase the EITC out more slowly or keep it for working parents.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late November 2025 and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it has sat for weeks with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Rashida Tlaib and seven original cosponsors introduced the End Child Poverty Act in the House on November 20, 2025.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the panel with jurisdiction over tax credits.
Ten House Democrats had signed on as cosponsors, and no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — had been taken as of the most recent action record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet. Families with children keep the current tax credits while the bill sits in committee, and nothing has changed for anyone.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; bill sits in committee

for.name: Rashida Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited seven original cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral — no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: There have been no votes, but every sponsor and cosponsor is a House Democrat and the committee that would act on it is run by Republicans, so any eventual split would likely follow party lines.

industries.note: The earned income and child tax credits are among the biggest drivers of paid tax preparation, so terminating them would trim that business — but the bill keeps the credits inside the tax code's filing system and adds new credits that still require a return, so much of the business survives.

analysis.trajectory: This bill faces very long odds. It is weeks old, has 10 cosponsors out of 435 members, sits in a committee controlled by the opposing party, and similar universal child allowance bills from prior Congresses never received a hearing. The most likely path is that it stays in committee and dies when the 119th Congress ends in January 2027, unless supporters attach it to broader tax legislation.
